item.title: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash
item.description:
Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash: Fast and cost-effective with longer clips

Today, we’re rolling out Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, and making it generally available across the Gemini API and Gemini for business. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash introduces native 15-second video creation, multi-turn conversational editing capabilities, and enhanced reference following. We have dropped the price 30% from Gemini Omni 1.1 making it available at $0.07 per second for 720p video.

Here’s an overview of what’s new:

Fast and cost-effective at scale

Beyond the lower price, the workflow keeps costs down: you can draft fast at 360p or 720p, fix a detail with a follow-up edit instead of re-generating the entire clip, and then upscale your best creations to 1080p or 4K.

Longer clips up to 15 seconds

You can now generate and edit videos natively up to 15 seconds long, up from 10 seconds with Omni 1.1. You can also specify duration in one-second increments from 3 to 15 seconds, giving you room to tell complete stories, create product explainers, or produce full social ad spots in a single generation.

Better reference adherence

You can guide generation combining character, product, or style images, short motion clips (up to three seconds), and audio cues — and Omni 1.2 Flash holds onto those details from start to finish. Faces, garments, packaging typography, and brand colors stay consistent across camera angles, making it easy to turn existing product photography or character sheets into virtual try-on clips, catalog spins, and branded video ads.

Combining one model photo with front-and-back product shots of three outfits, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates a 15-second virtual try-on sequence across 360-degree turns and match cuts while keeping the model’s identity and each garment’s cut, drape, and back details consistent.

More consistent results

You can maintain stronger character, object, and scene consistency from the first to the last frame, with less visual drift or morphing across motion and camera transitions. Whether you’re interpolating between a first and last keyframe, or extending a clip to build a longer sequence, products, characters, props, and environments stay consistent from shot to shot.

Given the same static studio lighting exhibition poster and five-layer animation prompt, Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash does not match the reference image as closely as 1.2 does. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash builds the poster sequentially layer by layer on the dusty-pink cyclorama rising the hexagonal plinth, assembling the ribbed glass, warm filament, faceted crystal, and coiled-cord letterforms for HALO, GLOW, and LUMEN, and locking every material, shadow, and typographic detail consistently through the final frame.

Easier editing in conversation

You can refine the same clip turn by turn — such as swapping a product or background, changing the lighting or weather, or switching the aspect ratio — instead of starting over from scratch. Multi-turn conversational editing works across full 15-second clips, making it easy to produce ad variants for different audiences and placements without re-briefing or re-generating.

Starting from one generated clip, multi-turn conversational prompts swap the background turn by turn — from a striped pavilion tent to an oak forest, a stable with a white horse, a market fair, and a stone castle — while keeping both characters’ performances, armor reflections, and camera framing intact.

More natural speech

You can generate scenes with more fluid, natural-sounding dialogue, clearer lip-sync, and distinct multi-speaker conditioning. This will show up whether you’re directing multi-character dialogue in Flow, creating video explainers in Gemini for business, or creating polished, pro videos with avatars, music and narration in Google Vids.

Conditioned on one conservatory scene image alongside four character, mouth, and one-second voice references, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash routes each sampled voice to the right character with expressive lip-sync and natural comedic timing across a 15-second animated scene.

More controllable, cinematic look

You can direct complex, continuous camera movements like sweeping FPV flythroughs to dramatic zoom-outs and orbits with significantly fewer unwanted jump cuts, steadier scale, and a more polished, cinematic look.

Guided by two architectural reference photos, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash directs one continuous FPV drone flight across the piazza, through the bronze doors, and up through the Pantheon’s coffered dome to the oculus with zero jump cuts.

Longer clips with smoother motion and tighter consistency

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates clips up to 15 seconds long that hold references together better than before. You can scroll through to see characters, text, and camera moves stay consistent across longer shots, multiple turns and transitions with no cuts.

Real-world results, from creatives to global brands

Businesses, startups, and creatives are already using Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash in their workflows. And for the first time, Gemini Omni is now generally available, backed by Google Cloud’s enterprise-grade infrastructure and security. Provisioned Throughput is available, and outputs carry an imperceptible SynthID watermark.

Get started with Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash

While development is ongoing to further improve things like fast sports action, rapid script changes and complex physics, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is ideal for businesses, developers, and creators producing videos at scale. You can get started with Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash today as it rolls out across Google’s products and developer platforms:

For developers using the Gemini API: Prototype in Google AI Studio, explore interactive starter apps, and check out the developer documentation and pricing. For businesses: Try it in the Google Cloud console, and build enterprise solutions with the API. For everyone using Google apps: Direct scenes and multi-turn edits in Flow, generate 15-second clips at no additional cost in Google Vids with a Google account or Google Workspace subscription, create 15-second videos in the Gemini app (rolling out to Google AI Ultra subscribers), and scale video campaigns in Google Ads.

item.title: University libraries are being swarmed by AI bots, putting public access at risk
item.description:
World

University libraries are being swarmed by AI bots, putting public access at risk One school says it was overwhelmed by more than 11,000 searches on Finnish music in just one day

Academic libraries are fighting off swarms of data-scraping bots — that are slowing or crashing sites meant for students, researchers and the public — as AI companies continue hunting for content to feed their large language models.

University libraries say entire collections are being knocked offline by persistent streams of unruly bots trying to access their archives, which include academic, historical and government documents.

"They're just out there on the internet, just bombarding us with trying to grab up as much material as possible," Jill Strykowski, cataloguing and government documents lead at San Jose State University, told CBC News.

The bots are used by both AI and third-party companies to scour websites and retrieve data, often to feed LLMs like Claude, Gemini and ChatGPT.

Libraries, museums and other cultural heritage institutions are prime targets because they have quality, vetted information that is generally not hidden behind paywalls or logins.

The bots are "causing an incredible amount of work and headache for every institution that does digitization work and every institution that is trying to make information openly available," Strykowski says.

Researchers found such reports started appearing in late 2024 across North America, Europe and Oceania and experts tell CBC News the problem continues to get worse.

And new challenges keep arising, says Dean Seeman, director of collections and digital infrastructure at University of Victoria Libraries.

"Sometimes the bot traffic gets so bad that it causes the sites to go down completely for a little while," he said.

Seeman says this creates a "real problem" for public access.

Regular people using library websites are now, effectively, in competition with infinite traffic from bot farms, says Peter Lewis, Canada Research Chair in Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence at Ontario Tech University.

"This is another instance of large, private companies making use of common-good public interest institutions in a way that's very extractive and just assumes that that stuff is available and is free — and then using it to be able to produce highly commercial models that then they can go and sell back to people," he said.

Workers enter data from an old document belonging to the McMillan Memorial Library during a digitization exercise at the Eastland Library in Nairobi on March 24, 2022. Libraries and other cultural heritage institutions are prime targets for AI bots. (Patrick Meinhardt/AFP/Getty Images)

Good bots and bad bots

Eric Hellman, executive director of Project Gutenberg — a U.S.-based volunteer organization that digitizes and archives cultural works and distributes eBooks — wrote in a blog last year that these bots, which he characterizes as poorly programmed "monstrosities," are "destroying open access" on the internet.

He tells CBC News that "everything's gotten worse" since he wrote that.

Hellman says the problem comes down to good bots and bad bots.

He explains that search engines like Google, and archiving sites like Internet Archive, use bots that follow robots.txt — voluntary sets of instructions on websites that tell them what they can and can't do, so they don't disrupt the site's functioning while gathering information.

AI scraping bots, on the other hand, sometimes ignore these rules and overwhelm websites — in some cases requesting thousands of documents a second and downloading them in every available format.

As an example, the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill reported last year that it received more than 11,000 searches for Finnish music from thousands of different internet addresses on the same day. The university said its library catalogue was periodically shutting out students, faculty and staff due to bot traffic.

And because one company or bot farm can work from thousands of IP addresses, Hellman says the old fix of blocking problematic IPs is no longer useful.

Michael Weinberg, co-director of GLAM-E, a collaborative effort focused on open-access policies for cultural institutions, is working to protect public access to information. (Submitted by Michael Weinberg)

He says Project Gutenberg is happy for its materials to be used as AI training data and even offers a one-click download of its entire library of books, "but the bots are too stupid to use it."

"Our material is almost all public domain material. It's exactly the sort of material that they should be training on," he said. "We just wish they would do it in a respectful way that doesn't take down websites."

Open access a 'huge benefit'

Some libraries have set up CAPTCHA challenges or other verification systems to weed out bots.

The problem is, those measures can also weed out the good bots, says Michael Weinberg, co-director of GLAM-E, a collaborative academic initiative at NYU Law School and the University of Warwick focused on open-access policies for cultural institutions.

Some libraries have also begun to require login credentials, a controversial move that those who spoke to CBC News say they want to avoid because it puts barriers on human access to things they believe should be easily accessible.

And as the scraping bots get more advanced, experts say they could also learn to work around these strategies.

The Anthropic logo is displayed at during the Dreamforce technology summit in San Francisco, on Sept. 17. AI firms have broadly argued that scraping publicly available data is permissible under fair use and in the public's best interest. (Carlos Barria/Reuters)

Major AI firms have argued that scraping publicly available data to train their models is permissible under fair use and in the public's best interest.

But faced with widespread criticism and copyright lawsuits, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Microsoft expressed support last week for honouring a single, standardized opt-out signal in a website's robots.txt file that could block their web crawlers from harvesting data.

Compliance would be voluntary, however, and the agreement leaves out problematic bots from third-party companies and smaller AI startups.

Used bookstores navigate 'suspicious' bulk orders amid AI book-shredding fears

How a small Canadian publisher is resisting the AI book wave

AI is making it harder for voters to get accurate information: Elections Canada chief

Weinberg says the digitization of valuable information has been a "fantastic" development for humanity — giving researchers, teachers and curious citizens easy access to resources that, 20 years ago, "would have required driving for flying or a special permission to get access."

Organizations like GLAM-E are trying to figure out long-term solutions to preserve that access for humans and helpful bots alike.

Right now, the bots create "a disincentive for libraries and other institutions to make parts of their collection available online," Weinberg said. "I think it's been a huge benefit to society that libraries and museums and other cultural institutions have put a huge amount of work into making their collections available."

People look at their laptops and in the main reading room of the New York Public Library on Oct. 5, 2016, in New York City. Increased bot traffic means regular people using library websites are effectively competing with infinite traffic from bot farms, says one expert. (Dominick Reuter/AFP/Getty Images)

item.title: MTG-I2 First Images
item.description:
Europe’s meteorological satellite agency, EUMETSAT has released the first image from the Flexible Combined Imager (FCI) on board Meteosat Third Generation Imager 2 (MTG-I2), just over two months after the satellite’s launch on 27 August 2026. The satellite will provide forecasters with high-resolution observations of Europe every 2.5 minutes. This unprecedented frequency will help forecasters monitor fast-developing weather hazards more closely and support earlier, more precise warnings.

Captured from geostationary orbit, some 36,000 km above the Earth, the image acquired on 20 October captures Europe, Africa and the Atlantic in remarkable detail, revealing intricate cloud formations stretching across the North Atlantic, contrasting with the largely clear skies over the Sahara.

While the full-disc image captures a single moment in time, an accompanying rapid-scan animation brings Europe’s weather to life, showing how cloud formations and weather systems evolve through observations taken just 2.5 minutes apart. This offers a glimpse of MTG-I2’s future operational service, which will enable meteorologists to monitor rapidly changing weather conditions over Europe more closely.

These first data follow the handover of MTG-I2 to EUMETSAT’s Mission Control Centre on 9 September, after the successful completion of the Launch and Early Orbit Phase. The satellite is still undergoing calibration and validation, working with the European Space Agency and European industry, to prepare it for operational service, which is expected to begin in the second quarter of 2027.

“This first image, and the animation, is a milestone for EUMETSAT and for our Member States,” EUMETSAT Director-General Phil Evans said. “Just two months after launch, MTG-I2 shows us what rapid scanning will make possible: a much timelier view of fast-developing weather over Europe. As extreme events become more frequent and intense, forecasters and emergency services will be able to see hazards evolve more precisely and act sooner.”

MTG-I2 will empower EUMETSAT’s Member States with a rapid scan service that will deliver high-resolution observations of the European continent every 2.5 minutes. By capturing changes in cloud formations at such rapid intervals, MTG-I2 will help forecasters follow the development of severe weather much more closely. This is especially valuable for fast-developing storms, which can bring heavy rainfall, hail, strong winds and flash floods. Timelier observations will also support earlier, more precise warnings and help emergency response during extreme events, including wildfires.

MTG-I2 is operated by EUMETSAT from its headquarters in Darmstadt, Germany. The satellite was developed by the European Space Agency with Thales Alenia Space as industry prime contractor, fulfilling the requirements set by EUMETSAT in consultation with the meteorological services of its Member States.

item.title: Lippitt-Knoster in Practice (Field Notes for Managing Complex Projects)
item.description:
"Lippitt-Knoster" is one of those things where if you've worked with me during the last 10 years, you've likely heard me mention it. You might even be reading this because I needed somewhere to point you. In which case, Hi! 👋

The Lippitt-Knoster Model for Managing Complex Change was originally written to describe a way of navigating large organizational shifts, but I’ve found that it’s also useful as a diagnosis tool for any kind of large and long-running project. After all, every project is a "change" in a microcosm. You might not have a complex organizational change to manage every day, but everyone is involved in long-running projects of some size and shape in a company. So that’s what I use it for, and it is useful indeed.

The beauty of the model is that you don’t need an MBA or a special issue of the Harvard Business Review to explain it. It says that any complex project requires six components to succeed, and if one or another is missing, you’ll have some specific and corresponding failure.

It can be summed up in a simple chart but also rewards you with some deeper insights as you apply it:

Vision is the purpose and endpoint of a project. Vision tells you where you’re going and why. If the vision is missing, there will be confusion about what is being done and why work is happening. Consensus is a team's agreement and alignment around the vision. If a team lacks consensus, people will not want to do the thing and they will sabotage you. Incentives are the motivation or reasons for why people support the work and prioritize it appropriately. If not everyone is incentivized properly, there will be resistance. Resistance is the passive sibling of sabotage. The Action Plan is the practical set of steps to get from vision to finish. If you lack an action plan, your team will experience a routine set of false starts and treadmills, which is another way of saying that it will look like work is happening but nothing actually moves forward. You won’t make progress. Resources are the organizational capacity (people, budget, time) needed to accomplish the work. Lacking resources is a close cousin to lacking skills; it leads to frustration in trying to do something you know you're capable of, but with an unrealistic set of operating constraints. Skills are the ability to do the work necessary to complete the project. If a team lacks the necessary skills, you'll have a lot of questions around if this work is possible, leading to anxiety.

Vision, consensus, and incentives are all Strategic Concerns. They involve abstract political work: ideas, relationships, people, and an understanding of the business. The action plan, skills, and resources are all Tactical Concerns. They are focused on the practical details of “how” something gets done.1

One mistake I often see people make is to focus primarily on one concern or the other. For example, a product manager or corporate strategist might spend too much time focused on the strategic side of things without understanding if the team or company is able to execute. Consequently, their ability to build consensus will be negatively impacted by not knowing what is possible or probable. Line managers and software engineers typically make the opposite mistake. They focus too much on the ‘how’ instead of the ‘why’. They’ll prove that something is possible and how it can be done, without realizing that sometimes the team or business doesn't want to do the thing they’re proposing. Neither myopia ends in a successful project.

The order of the model components matters – they flow into each other – but can be managed in either direction. For example: you might start with a vision, build consensus, arrange the right incentives for everyone to act, create a plan, provide adequate resources and timeline to accomplish that plan, and make sure it is staffed with people who have the skills to execute on it. Easy peasy!

You could also navigate the components the other way, working through a series of questions: is something possible? Do skills exist to accomplish the thing? Do those skills (people) have excess capacity that can be allocated to this idea? Can it be done without budget? Can that group of people be small enough that they organically develop their own plans? And if so, are they incentivized to take on this kind of work outside their daily responsibilities? Does it need sign-off from anyone? If you’ve found confirmatory answers along the way, congratulations: you can carve out a secret R&D initiative within your team or your company. (This is also 'effectuation' in practice.)

You can also read the model from the perspectives of both cause and effect. Reading it one way creates a checklist before kicking off any major work: “Here are the six prerequisites for success, are we all set?” (A causal, prescriptive reading – given starting parameters, what will be the end result?) Reading it backwards turns it into a troubleshooting tool. For example, if someone comes to you mid-project complaining that "We keep going in circles and the team is anxious! What can I do?" you might look at the model and respond, "Well of course! You don't have an action plan. Or maybe, it hasn't been adequately distributed and communicated and people feel that they lack the skills to accomplish something so big. Let's break it down into manageable pieces that we do have the skills for." It’s pretty quick to go between looking at the failure states and looking at the necessary components to diagnose what’s going on with a project. (A diagnostic reading, reasoning backwards.)

The model is a fantastic tool for making sense of things. But that leaves the hard work to start after you've made sense of things. How do you drive consensus? How do you align folks around a vision? How do you build up skills, or break down big projects into smaller pieces for which skills exist? How do you win resources, or align incentives?

Some of those answers are obvious, but most are not. Many of the answers are best understood as the manifestation of tacit expertise — a ‘feeling’ for the right move in any particular context, a form of expertise that comes from having been around the block a few times.

And like with most tacit expertise, you’ll find that there are no one-size-fits-all answers to any scenario, but there are plenty of good practices and useful observations.

So here are some of mine:

Strategic Concerns

The most common and important questions that come up after someone lays out a vision are “Why should we do this?” and permutations around the follow-up details. If you see those questions, that’s “confusion”, which is another way of saying you’ve presented a fantasy instead of a vision (or perhaps, the vision is missing entirely). That’s because many people confuse vision for having a colorful and inspiring imagination, making their picture too colorful, unrealistically grand, or too far off.2

My experience is that you make more progress by simply providing adequate context and letting people derive their own vision. The art of context is giving people breadcrumbs to get from where you are today to where you want to be in the future, and giving them some good reasons to follow those breadcrumbs with you. There’s nothing more effective than a self-motivated team that thinks they’re the ones who came up with the idea, that they saw what things could be like. That’s vision.

Similarly, consensus is a straightforward concept, but strangely elusive in most organizations. Any organization beyond a certain age and size will typically have a 'minimally viable consensus' while practically being at odds with itself. Departments often turn into silos with their own internal logic for what should happen. Job security encourages teams to think about what’s best for them instead of for the company. And companies don’t do a great job tying “what’s best for the company” with “what’s best for the individuals within, or the communities around”,3 which makes most employment mercenary: people naturally find a balance between what they’re paid and how much to care about the thing in question. (In that sense, incorporated businesses are kind of like democracy: a bad choice, but among the best of the options available for coordinating large groups of people to accomplish things.)

Recognizing that, one amateur mistake people make is trying to build consensus in a group setting. It just doesn't happen that way. You’re either going to have everyone nodding along and afraid to say their piece in front of everyone else, or you’re going to have one guy (and it’s usually a guy – sorry, my dudes) start pulling some “what about”-ism and dragging the conversation into a black hole of details that you never intended to argue about but find yourself frustratingly debating anyway.

In either scenario, the meeting will end without consensus.

In Japanese business culture there is a concept called “nemawashi”, which translates roughly to “tending to the roots” or “laying the groundwork”. It’s a good analogy because the practice of creating consensus requires a lot of political skill, footwork, trust-building, and private conversation. It means giving people space to tell you everything that’s wrong with your idea, finding ways to address those concerns, and making sure everyone is aligned before the alignment actually happens. The group meeting when everyone signs off in agreement should be the result of careful stage management — you should know and have already addressed everyone’s concerns, including second-order effects of how addressing one person’s issues will impact others.

There should be no surprises; it is theater, not improv.

That said, you might not be able to get to consensus. Perhaps your boss wants the “thing” to happen but there’s another department that’s actively against it. Maybe you're encroaching on their turf, or it will reduce their capacity in some zero-sum resource bucket. Maybe they just have a different perspective on the world and the approaches the business should take. Maybe you've wandered into a long-running feud and this project is just one of many different battles being waged. Who knows, people can be both petty and complicated!

If you can't get their buy-in, they will sabotage it in all sorts of creative ways. Because sabotage and resistance are close cousins and are political (in the sense of not being open conflict), monographs on activism and subterfuge can be read as useful primers. Consider James C. Scott's Weapons of the Weak and the OSS's Simple Sabotage Field Manual for what kinds of foot dragging, malicious compliance, noncompliance, evasion, sowing confusion, slander, useless meetings, arbitrary hurdles, revisiting decisions, and moving goalposts to expect.

My advice for these scenarios is to try one of two things. Your first option is to get to the bottom of why there is no consensus and figure out if you’re in a position to address that root cause. Often, you’re not in a position to address those things; if you pursue resolution, you’re going to use up a lot of your political capital or burn out trying to get the project moving forward. And success can be fleeting – projects can continue to be sabotaged even after launch. I once had a project launch only to have all of its resources immediately pulled, forcing its premature death.

Not even chief executives are immune to this; sometimes the solution to a lack of consensus and active sabotage is to simply fire the people in disagreement. (Obviously, use this technique sparingly — you’re scorching the earth.)

So I recommend most people take the second approach, which is to just drop it. Move on. It’s a lost cause. Don’t be the sailor with a bucket trying to dump water off this Titanic. Quitting things and dropping things is a totally acceptable thing to do; life isn’t a video game where you’re striving for 100% completeness on every side quest. Move on to things where you’re actually making a difference.

But let’s say everyone agrees. Now you need to make sure that things are prioritized appropriately. You’re not going to make any progress if this is low on everyone’s priority list. So you incentivize teams and people.

Positive incentives typically work better than negative incentives, but most people are not in a position to offer meaningful (financial) incentives to push a project forward. Instead, you can rely on horse-trading (“if you help me move this project forward, I’ll help with your thing”), you can help people resolve their problems, and you can paint a compelling-enough end-state that people also want to reach that goal with you.

Otherwise, people are going to be resistant, which is a passive form of sabotage: sabotage without commitment, or general apathy. It might not even be malicious. It’s just… well, you’re just one more project for people to care about and work on. Why should they do it above all else?

And more importantly, resistance can turn into sabotage when incentives are not just missing, but misaligned. Misaligned incentives can break consensus when you're sweating the details.

Tactical Concerns

Now, let’s say you figured out the strategic bits and you’re working through the implementation portion. Some projects are simple enough that you can just describe what needs to be done, and you can count those requirements on a single maimed hand. We’re not talking about those projects.

Any complex-enough project requires coordination of requirements, dependencies, timelines, people, and other details. I’ve written a bit about those issues in “When Everything is Important But Nothing Is Getting Done”, so I don’t want to retread too much ground.

But one thing worth highlighting is how skills and anxiety are coupled, and how to navigate a lack of skills. Any ambitious project is at some point going to run into a lack of skills or prior experience because the work wouldn't be ambitious if you'd done it before. So in many regards, it is an existential question for any project: are you and your team able to do what needs to be done? If not, you’ll get a very stressed team, or you’ll get a simulacrum of what you expected.

There are ways to compensate for a lack of skills. I rely on three techniques:

First is up-skilling people. Education, mentorship, and training are effective ways to turn juniors into seniors, low-skilled employees into high-skilled employees. While there are a variety of documented techniques for this (see: accelerated expertise, tactical decision games), the caveats are that (a) this typically takes longer than the time-span of a single project and (b) you need to find people who are interested in learning.

So the second technique is atomization: break the requirements into smaller pieces that meet the level of skill available rather than trying to get people to rise to the required level. Instead of making everyone work harder, just make the requirements easier. Instead of asking people to “cut database reads by 50%” or “create a capacity forecasting model for the next 12 months” (where they may not even know where to start), give them smaller tasks and directions for what to do to accomplish that. Point folks in the right direction, explain the what and the why, turn big asks into a series of steps, a recipe to accomplish something. This is in itself a form of teaching, and it is more project-sized (see what I did there?).

The third technique is to roll up your sleeves and contribute. I’ve learned from many effective leaders that there is no work below your pay grade. What makes many great leaders "great" is their willingness to spend extra time doing “glue” work, filling in the holes between roles, and making sure all assumptions are bridged back to real expectations. They are never too good to personally write up a project document, to manage a tracker, to make sure that people are talking to each other. They often know as much or more about the details than subject matter experts, but they don't needlessly meddle – they support where needed and use gaps as up-skilling opportunities.

Much of the work of compensating for skills gaps is directly translatable into managing budget, time, and effort tradeoffs to navigate the “resources” component of Lippitt-Knoster. And your ability to solve for skills and resources directly translates back into the specific action plan you need to put together. For example: you may decide not to spend $100,000 on a vendor because you can reverse engineer a single feature you need for a project, but you need to add time to the plan for that.

These considerations become a calculus of risks, rewards, and effort, which in turn underpins the strategic portions that we talked about earlier: sure, you might think you can lead a team to rebuild the hot new vendor in house in two months, but have you earned organizational political capital to place those chips on the table?

So there you have it, Lippitt-Knoster in practice. Lead on!

1 - This grouping is not present in most Lippitt-Knoster model descriptions I’ve come across; it is my own humble contribution. The order I'm presenting it in is also my contribution – the order in Mary Lippit's original 1987 model is quite different, for reasons I couldn't discern.

2 - A realistic vision that is too far into the future is its own type of risk – every day presents new opportunities for conditions to change, starting conditions to be led astray. The likelihood of any far-off future has too many compounding variables... too many things have to go right and be true for it to be reliable enough to pin your hopes to.

3 - These things are usually at odds with each other. There's a big literature about how "equity" is a tool to get employees to care about corporate success, but most startup equity goes to zero; for the average employee, a bonus or a pay raise is more useful. Public company equity presents a different issue: it is dependent on public market behavior, and less on your individual ability to impact it – being in a public company, you're likely one of thousands-plus of employees.

RIP Cybertruck
item.description:
Elon Musk, in a post on X, has officially called time on the Cybertruck, stating that “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”

Produced for less than four years, the polarizing pickup is seemingly dying as it lived, with the news being greeted in a flurry of replies in praise of the EV as well as deriding it. James Star, claiming to be a Tesla employee, posted that it was “the saddest news! Cybertruck (was) the best car Tesla sold,” right next to a user called Captain Ford who simply replied to Musk with “Fuck that shitbox.”

Tesla has not responded to WIRED’s request for comment and clarification that the Cybertruck will no longer be made at all. The Cybertruck is exclusively made at Gigafactory Texas, as this is apparently the only Tesla facility equipped with the machinery required to manufacture the truck’s unique stainless steel body, which supposedly started to rust in some cases.

Despite whipping up a fevered number of reservations—allegedly more than a million according to Musk, who at the end of 2023 crowed that demand was “off the charts!”—the truck failed to sell, shifting less than 50,000 units in total by March last year.

EVWire cites Kelley Blue Book data suggesting that Tesla sold 11,586 Cybertrucks in the first three quarters of this year in the US, down 28 percent year-over-year, adding that Musk’s announcement post came about 80 minutes after Tesla raised US Cybertruck prices and paused new orders for the entry-level Dual-Motor AWD version.

The Cybertruck proved not only to be wildly unpopular, it was also beset by troubles before it even reached customers. In 2023, WIRED covered a leaked Tesla report dated January 25, 2022, that showed the Cybertruck had basic design flaws, and that the preproduction “alpha” version was struggling with problems with its suspension, body sealing, noise levels, handling, and braking.

In November 2019, when Musk stepped onto a stage in California to launch his new cyberpunk-styled electric pickup, he decided to demonstrate the strength of the “unbreakable” glass windows by hurling a steel ball at them. In what has now entered into public relations folklore, the demo truck’s windows smashed not once, but twice. Musk swore, then joked: “There’s room for improvement.”

There most certainly was. In April 2024, a recall was issued for the Cybertruck because its accelerator pedal pad could come loose and get trapped by interior trim, which had the frightening potential of pushing the car to full speed.

In March last year, Tesla had to recall nearly all the Cybertrucks it had then produced because a stainless steel trim panel could become detached from the vehicle while driving, blaming the problem on the wrong type of glue, a new adhesive “not prone to environmental embrittlement.”

Back in May this year, Cybertrucks were struck down by the wrong type of grease, which meant that their wheels could potentially fall off. In what was then the EV’s 11th recall, it was declared that the Rear Wheel Drive (RWD) Cybertruck Long Range model might have faulty brake rotors. In a notice posted by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, Tesla stated that “brake rotor stud holes may crack and allow the stud to separate from the wheel hub.” Such a situation might have seen some RWD Cybertruck owners merrily driving along only to then be disconcertingly overtaken by their own wheels.

Musk even tried to get President Donald Trump to buy one of his Cybertrucks, creating an impromptu Tesla showroom on the White House South Lawn, no less. But, sadly, even President Trump must have smelt something was off about the truck as instead he shunned the pickup and opted for a 200-mph Model S Plaid in ultra red, clearly impressed with the interior, remarking that “Everything’s computer!”

At the end of 2024, Karl Brauer, executive analyst at car ranking service iSeeCars, told WIRED that he’d calculated that the Cybertruck’s six recalls to date at the time made the EV “worse than 91 percent” of all other 2024 vehicles.

Yet, despite supposedly being so unreliable, the Cybertruck did find a small but loyal audience. WIRED profiled a number of owners last year, all fervently in love with their vehicles, but who were periodically forced to endure insults and taunts that they were Nazis, perhaps referring to an on-stage gesture Musk made at the start of 2025.

However, despite evidence seemingly to the contrary, Musk claims he is killing the Cybertruck, not because of its unreliability and staggering unpopularity, but because he wishes to focus instead on Cybercab, an autonomous EV that is central to Tesla’s robotaxi ambitions but itself has had a rocky start.

Currently operating in Austin only, with a fleet supposedly numbered only in the hundreds, Musk apparently wants to ramp up production dramatically since he confirmed on an earnings call the first cab came off the line in February.

Musk sees Cybercab as very much the vision of Tesla’s future. The CEO has even said that Tesla should no longer be regarded as an automaker but as a robotics and autonomous vehicle company. “Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab,” Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill said on X.
